problem: VLN-CE models are trained with human-height (~1.7 m) observations, but low quadruped robots (~30 cm eye height) suffer large performance drops, and depth-based waypoint predictors generalize poorly to complex real scenes. Occlusions at ground level also make local observations insufficient.
motivation: Human instructions are issued from a high line of sight, while robots such as the Xiaomi Cyberdog see mostly ground-level obstacles. Raising the sensor would hurt passability in narrow spaces. Existing VLN work had not studied this viewpoint-height generalization gap, which matters for real deployment.
key_idea: Scale up waypoint-predictor training on low-height renderings using connectivity graphs from HM3D, Gibson and MP3D, and add a learned attention-weighted multi-view fusion for ghost nodes so the policy can use earlier unobstructed views.
insight: Re-training the waypoint predictor matters more than re-training the navigator under low viewpoints: ETPNav with a re-trained WP and frozen navigator reaches 39% SR on val-unseen, versus 32% for a re-trained navigator with a frozen WP (both from 21%). Scaling WP data 22x raises the open-space rate by about 8 points. Re-training on low-view data alone still leaves a gap to high-view results, so an architectural fix (adaptive multi-view gathering) helps further.
method: Low-height waypoint dataset: uses ScaleVLN connectivity graphs over 800 HM3D, 491 Gibson and 61 MP3D scans, with depth (and RGB) rendered at 80 cm in Habitat, giving 212,924 samples (22.02x the original) with distance and orientation labels for waypoint supervision.
Waypoint prediction network: a Transformer over panoramic view features predicts candidate waypoints, re-trained on the scaled low-view data (RGBD or depth-only variants compared).
Topological planner: follows ETPNav, with a topo map of visited, current and ghost nodes, a global action space and node pruning.

Multi-view Information Gathering: a trainable transformer encoder layer applies self-attention over the multiple view features observed for a ghost node, then a Linear+Softmax weighted sum replaces the plain average to give the ghost-node feature.
Real robot rig: Xiaomi Cyberdog with a RealSense D455 on a programmable motor rotating in 30° steps to capture 12 images as a panorama, with models running on a laptop RTX 3080.

numbers_note: Metrics in the paper are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.64), so they are kept as printed rather than converted to percent. The in-text claim that the model outperforms baselines on all splits does not fully match the tables, since ETPNav has lower NE in two real-world scenes.
results: Under low line-of-sight, GVNav gets 64/55 SR (val-seen/unseen) and 56/45 SPL. It beats the re-trained ETPNav (58/52 SR, 50/43 SPL) and BEVBert (51/47 SR). On the real Cyberdog it achieves SR of 0.28-0.40 across four scenes, above ETPNav (0.20-0.28) and BEVBert.
limitations: Real-world evaluation is small (25 instructions per scene, 4 scenes) and needs a rotating-camera panoramic rig, with 12 captures per step.
Instructions are still written from a human viewpoint. The paper does not address instruction mismatch, and the multi-view gathering module has no dedicated ablation.
Real-world gains over ETPNav are modest, and NE is worse in some scenes.
